t.5.36.1: Then that tiger among monkeys, skilled in speech, delighted by those words, having heard that speech, spoke to Sītā.
t.5.36.2: O queen of auspicious appearance, what you have spoken is fitting, befitting the nature of a woman and the modesty of virtuous women.
t.5.36.3: But womanhood, which governs me, is surely not capable of crossing the ocean, so vast and stretching a hundred yojanas in length.
t.5.36.4: And the second reason that you state, O Jānakī endowed with modesty, namely, 'I ought not to suffer the touch of anyone other than Rāma'
t.5.36.5: O queen, this is fitting for you, the wife of that great-souled one; for who else but you, O queen, would speak such words?
t.5.36.6: And Kākutstha shall hear everything, without anything left out: all that you have done, O queen, and all that you have spoken in my presence.
t.5.36.8: Because Laṅkā is hard to enter, because the great ocean is hard to cross, and indeed because of my own capability, this was proposed by me.
t.5.36.7: For many reasons, O Devī, out of the wish to do what is dear to Rāma, and with a mind overflowing with affection, I have spoken these words.
t.5.36.9: I wish to reunite you this very day with the kinsman of the Raghus. I have said this out of deep affection for my master and out of devotion, and not for any other reason.
t.5.36.10: If you do not dare to go with me, O blameless lady, then give me a token of recognition, one that Rāghava will surely recognize.
t.5.36.11: Thus addressed by Hanumān, Sītā, who resembled a daughter of the gods, spoke softly, her words choked with tears.
t.5.36.12: But you should tell him this excellent token of recognition, dear to me: what happened then at the north-eastern foot of the mountain Citrakūṭa.
t.5.36.14: Having sported in the groves of its gardens, fragrant with many kinds of flowers, I, still wet with water, sat down upon your lap.
t.5.36.13: As I was dwelling in a hermitage of ascetics, in that region of the hermitage of the Siddhas, rich in abundant roots, fruits and water, not far from the Mandākinī…
t.5.36.15: And in his turn, the elder brother of Bharata fell asleep on my lap.
t.5.36.16: Then a crow, intent on meat, began pecking all around, and raising a clod of earth I kept driving that crow away.
t.5.36.17: And that crow, tearing at me, kept hovering right there; the crow, eater of offerings, eager for food, would not desist from my flesh.
t.5.36.18: As I, enraged at the bird, was tugging at my girdle and my garment was slipping down, it was then indeed that I was seen by you.
t.5.36.20: And when I was weary, I lay down again in your lap as you sat there; and though I was angry, you, filled with delight, soothed me.
t.5.36.19: Then, laughed at by you, I was angry and ashamed; torn by that greedy black one after it had fed on me, I came to you.
t.5.36.21: O lord, you saw me, enraged by the crow, my face streaming with tears, slowly wiping my eyes.
t.5.36.22: Enraged like a venomous serpent and hissing, you spoke these words: “O you whose thighs are like an elephant’s trunk, by whom has the space between your breasts been wounded? Who is it that plays with an angry five-headed serpent?”
t.5.36.23: Then, looking about, you caught sight of that very crow, its sharp claws smeared with blood, standing right before me and facing me.
t.5.36.24: That crow, they say, was the son of Śakra, the best of flying creatures, swiftly roaming the regions of the earth and equal to the wind in speed.
t.5.36.25: Then the mighty-armed one, his eyes rolling with anger, set his mind on a cruel resolve against that crow, O best among the wise.
t.5.36.26: Taking a blade from the mat of darbha grass, you charged it with Brahmā's weapon; and it, blazing like the fire at the end of time, flared up as it faced the bird.
t.5.36.27: You hurled that blazing reed at the crow. Then, pursued by it, the black one fled in various directions; seeking protection, he wandered through this entire world.
t.5.36.28: Abandoned by his father, by all the gods and by the great seers, he wandered through the three worlds and came to you alone for refuge.
t.5.36.29: Finding no peace anywhere in the worlds, he came to you alone for refuge. O Kākutstha, you, the giver of refuge, out of compassion protected him as he lay fallen on the ground, a seeker of refuge, though he deserved death.
t.5.36.30: You, that same one, said to him as he came back worn out and dejected: “The Brahma weapon cannot be made fruitless, so let it be said what it shall strike.”
t.5.36.31: Then he destroyed the right eye of that crow.
t.5.36.32: Then he, having paid homage to you and to King Daśaratha, and being dismissed by you, O hero, returned to his own abode.
t.5.36.33: For my sake the Brahmāstra was hurled even at a mere crow; why then, O lord of the earth, do you pardon him who carried me away from you?
t.5.36.34: Therefore, O bull among men, put forth great effort and show compassion toward me; that non-cruelty is the highest dharma I have heard from you yourself.
t.5.36.35: I know you to be of great valour, great energy and great strength, one whose limits cannot be reached, imperturbable, like the ocean in depth, the lord of the earth together with its seas, equal to Vāsava.
t.5.36.37: Neither the Nāgas nor the Gandharvas, neither the Asuras nor the hosts of Maruts are able to withstand the onslaught of Rāma in battle.
t.5.36.36: Being thus the foremost of those who know weapons, full of courage and mighty as well, why do you not discharge your weapon against the Rākṣasas, O Rāghava?
t.5.36.38: If that valiant one has any anxious concern for me, why does he not bring the rākṣasas to destruction with his sharp arrows?
t.5.36.39: Or why does Lakṣmaṇa, the scorcher of foes, the mighty and heroic one, not take his brother's command and rescue me?
t.5.36.40: If those two tigers among men, whose splendour equals that of Vāyu and Indra, are unassailable even by the gods, why do they neglect me?
t.5.36.41: Without doubt there is some great misdeed of mine alone, since those two scorchers of foes, though capable, do not look after me.
t.5.36.42: On my behalf, ask after the well-being of him, the lord of the world, whom the noble-minded Kausalyā bore, and salute him with your head bowed.
t.5.36.43: Garlands and all kinds of jewels, and those beloved, excellent women, and a sovereignty hard to obtain even on the wide earth.
t.5.36.45: Lion-shouldered, mighty-armed, high-minded and pleasing to behold, he follows his brother Kākutstha, protecting him in the forest.
t.5.36.44: He who, having honoured and won the favour of his father and mother, followed Rāma into exile, he through whom Sumitrā is blessed with a noble son, that righteous-souled one who out of devotion gave up unsurpassed comfort.
t.5.36.46: The heroic Lakṣmaṇa, who conducts himself toward Rāma as toward a father and treats me as a mother, did not know at that time that I was being carried away.
t.5.36.48: Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma's brother, is ever dearer to him than I am; whatever burden he is yoked to, that the valiant one carries to the end.
t.5.36.47: The prince, who waits upon his elders, is glorious and capable, not given to much talk, foremost among those dear to me, and like my father-in-law.
t.5.36.49: Lakṣmaṇa, gentle, ever pure, capable and dear to Rāma, seeing whom Rāghava did not even remember his aged and noble father, should be asked after his welfare for my sake, in my own words.
t.5.36.50: And say this to my lord, the heroic Rāma, again and again: 'I shall hold on to my life for one month, O son of Daśaratha; beyond that month I would not live. By the truth I tell you this.'
t.5.36.51: O hero, you ought to rescue me, held captive through treachery by Rāvaṇa of evil deeds, just as Kauśikī was rescued from Pātāla.
t.5.36.52: Then, untying the divine and auspicious crest-jewel that was kept in her garment, Sītā gave it to Hanumān, saying, "It is to be given to Rāghava."
t.5.36.53: Then the hero, having received that peerless jewel, fitted it onto his finger, for his arm could not pass through it.
t.5.36.54: The foremost of monkeys took the jewel, saluted Sītā, and walked around her reverently, keeping her to his right; then, bowing low, he stood at her side.
t.5.36.55: Filled with the great joy born of seeing Sītā, he went to Rāma in his heart, though in body he remained where he stood.
t.5.36.56: Taking that excellent and very precious jewel, which the daughter of King Janaka had worn on account of its power, he, his mind at ease, like one set free after being buffeted by the wind of the great mountain, set out on his return.
